name: Slab serif
summary: Heavy, square serifs on a sturdy letter with low contrast. Born on the poster in industrial Britain, it carries a loud, solid and practical voice, and modern text cuts serve screens and typewriters as well.

philosophy.core_thesis: A letter for a loud and busy world must be heavy, square and hard to break.
design_principles: Make the serifs at least 0.6 of the stem thickness and square at the ends.
Keep the stroke contrast at 1.0–1.8:1, measured on the o.
Use no bracket (the Egyptian) or a small one (the Clarendon), and keep the choice the same in all letters.
Hold the x-height at 0.66–0.76 of the cap height.
Set titles in a bold or heavy weight; text cuts use a regular weight with serifs 0.6–0.8 of the stem.
Space the letters a little loose: the slabs need 0.01–0.02 em more room than a sans.
anti_patterns: Tight negative tracking that makes the slabs touch
Mixing bracketed and unbracketed slabs in one setting

classification.note: The British Standard (BS 2961) calls the class Slab-serif; the Clarendon type with brackets is sometimes filed as a sub-class of its own.

anatomy.contrast: Low: the thin parts are 0.55–1.0 of the stem.
anatomy.serifs: Thick and rectangular, 0.6–1.0 of the stem; bracketed in the Clarendon type, with no bracket in the Egyptian.
anatomy.terminals: Flat or slab terminals on c, f and r; a ball on the a in some Clarendons.
anatomy.aperture: Moderate to open in modern text cuts.
anatomy.key_letters: A two-storey a with a slab on the foot, a t with a slab on the left of the cross-bar, and an M with four slabs at the base.

metrics.x_height: The x-height is 0.66–0.76 of the cap height and about 0.45–0.53 of the em.
metrics.contrast: The side of the o is 1.0 to 1.8 times as thick as its top.
metrics.width: Medium to wide; the mean advance of a to z is 0.49–0.56 em.
metrics.figures: Lining figures, tabular in most digital cuts.

setting.text_sizes: Set text cuts at 9–11 pt in print and 15–18 px on screen.
setting.display_sizes: Set bold and heavy weights at 24–120 pt for posters and headlines.
setting.leading: Set the leading at 1.4–1.6 times the size for text, and 1.0–1.15 for headlines.
setting.tracking: Set +0.01 to +0.02 em in text, and 0 to −0.01 em in large headlines.
setting.case_and_features: Use capitals for short poster lines; tabular figures for prices and tables.

pairing.rule: Pair it with a sans of the same era or skeleton, and keep the slab for headlines or for short text.

pairs.role: sans for body text and labels
pairs.why: Both come from the nineteenth-century poster, so the voices agree.
A modern slab such as Zilla Slab shares its open, written skeleton.

faces.designer: Robert Besley for the Fann Street Foundry

reference_faces.note: Roboto Slab and Arvo are geometric slabs with no bracket; Zilla Slab is a humanist slab. No open font in this record is a strict Clarendon.

emotion.target_response: Solidity and directness: the reader feels a practical, confident voice that is easy to trust.

avoid_when: The brief asks for delicacy, luxury or high fashion.
The page needs a quiet text face for a long book.

modifiers.how: Thin the serifs to 0.3 of the stem, add brackets, and raise the contrast to 3:1.
Remove the slabs; keep the low contrast, the weight and the industrial voice.

sources.title: Robert Bringhurst, The Elements of Typographic Style (Hartley & Marks, 4th ed. 2012)
